report:
You are correct — the evidence strongly indicates that arthroscopy does **not** help with osteoarthritis of the knee. Here is a summary of the key evidence:

**1. Landmark placebo-controlled trial (Moseley et al., 2002, NEJM)**
The pivotal study was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*. Patients with knee osteoarthritis were assigned to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or sham (placebo) surgery. At no point over two years did the real surgery groups report less pain or better function than the placebo group. This was a striking finding — sham surgery worked just as well. (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259)

**2. Cochrane systematic review (2022)**
A Cochrane review assessing arthroscopic surgery (debridement, partial meniscectomy, or both) versus placebo or non-surgical treatment for degenerative knee disease found no clinically meaningful benefit. It concluded that arthroscopic knee surgery provides no important benefit in pain or function for patients with degenerative knee disease. (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full)

**3. BMJ systematic review and meta-analysis (2015)**
A BMJ meta-analysis of randomized trials found that arthroscopic knee surgery was associated with only a small, clinically insignificant pain reduction in the short term and no benefit in physical function, while carrying potential harms. (https://www.bmj.com/content/bmj/350/bmj.h2747.full.pdf)

**4. Clinical practice guideline (BMJ, 2017)**
An international guideline panel strongly recommended **against** arthroscopic knee surgery for patients with degenerative knee disease, noting that the evidence showed no benefit and potential harm. (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline)

**Conclusion:** Multiple high-quality randomized trials, systematic reviews, and clinical guidelines consistently show that arthroscopic surgery (lavage, debridement, or partial meniscectomy) offers no meaningful benefit over placebo or conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis. Despite this, the procedure remains commonly performed, likely due to financial incentives and entrenched practice patterns.
